coach_says: Nc6 is a perfectly playable developing move against this offbeat opening. It does block your c-pawn, so ...c5 is no longer available against a later d4, which is why ...c5 or ...Nf6 are slightly more flexible, but this is a matter of taste, not a mistake.
also: keep the c-pawn free in d-pawn openings

coach_says: Castling here is sound: your king gets safe and your rook comes towards the centre. Taking on c6 first and swapping the dark-squared bishops was a touch more precise, but there is nothing here you need to change.

You had to win the piece back and Nxc3 does that safely. Recapturing with the b-pawn was slightly better because it hits the bishop on b4 and keeps your e2 knight free to jump to g3 and chase the f5 bishop, but both recaptures leave a level, healthy game.
1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is a fully respectable answer to 1.e4. It prepares ...d5 to challenge White's centre with solid support. Nothing to fix here.

Taking on c5 is a reasonable choice that opens lines on the queenside. f4, hitting Black's centre and opening the f-file for your rook, was a little more energetic, but the difference is small and the game stays balanced.
Rae1+ is a strong move: Black's king is stuck in the middle and you bring a rook to the open e-file with check. Bg6+ and Qxc7 were just as good. Keep hunting that king.
also: attack the king stuck in the centre

coach_says: Nc3 is natural development, though it lets Black pin it with ...Bb4 and gain time with ...d4 against your knight. Your real issue is the early Qf3 that has given Black a strong centre; the knight move itself costs very little.
Kd2 is fine: your king heads for the queenside to deal with Black's b- and c-pawns. The position remains a draw with correct play, and several moves hold just as well.
h4 is the best move. Your king is safe on c2, so throwing the kingside pawns forward with g5 next to open lines at Black's king is exactly the right plan.
also: pawn storm on the castled king

coach_says: Be7 is about as good as anything here; Black is already in trouble because White will open the centre with exd5 while your king is uncastled. Developing and castling as quickly as possible was the right idea.
c3 is a reasonable plan to build a d4 centre, but it lets Black hit your bishop with ...d5. Nc3 develops a piece and keeps more control of d5. The difference is small and the game is level.
also: ...d5 gains time on the c4 bishop

coach_says: 2.Bg5 is an offbeat but playable system. Taking the bishop out before Nf3 leaves b2 a bit loose to ...c5 and ...Qb6 ideas, so the main moves Nf3 and c4 are a little more solid, but this is a question of opening choice rather than a mistake.
You are a rook down in a lost queen endgame, so checks like Qd5+ are as good as anything; keep checking and hope for a mistake or a perpetual. The damage was done much earlier.

When the e5 pawn kicked your knight, Ng4 sent it away from the centre: after h3 its only safe square is h6, on the edge, and White follows with d5 and d6 to gain space and time. Nd5 was the right square: it is central and no white pawn can ever attack it there, since White has no c- or e-pawn able to reach it. When a pawn attacks your knight, look first for a strong central square before a raid on the side.
concept: knight to the centre, not the rim

coach_says: With your king on d8 and White's rook on d1, ...d6 opens the d-file towards your own king. After Nb6, hitting your rook on a8, White plays exd6 and gets a passed pawn on d6, backed by the rook, that cramps your bishops and your king. Keep the d7 pawn as a shield and develop the queenside instead, with ...b5 and ...Rb8 or ...Ra7, before changing the centre.
concept: opening the file to your own king
